# Data {#sec-data}

## Simulated data {#sec-simdata}

We built the simulation the way the course's simulation deck recommends: one
function, `gen_data()`, takes as arguments exactly the factors we vary, and
the true model is fixed inside it.

Each simulated data set has five predictors $x_1, \dots, x_5$, drawn
independently from $N(0, 1)$. The outcome comes from a logistic model
[@islr2, eq. 4.2]:

$$
P(y = 1 \mid x) = \frac{e^{\eta}}{1 + e^{\eta}}, \qquad
\eta = \beta_0 + s\,(x_1 - x_2 + 0.5\,x_3 - 0.5\,x_4 + 0\cdot x_5).
$$

The multiplier $s$ controls *separation*. A larger $s$ means larger slopes,
so the two classes overlap less and the problem is easier. The fifth
predictor has a slope of zero, so it is pure noise and gives the lasso
something to remove. For every row we also keep the true probability
$P(y = 1 \mid x)$, stored as `p.true`. The models never see it; we use it only
for the Bayes benchmark described in @sec-metrics.

To make the positive class rare we lower the intercept $\beta_0$ and leave
the slopes alone. This keeps "rarer" separate from "harder": at a given
separation, the relationship between the predictors and the log-odds is the
same at every prevalence. For each prevalence $\pi$ and separation $s$ we
need the $\beta_0$ that makes the average of $P(y = 1 \mid x)$ equal to $\pi$.
Since $x^\top\beta$ is normal with mean 0 and variance $s^2 \sum_j \beta_j^2$,
we approximated that average with $10^6$ normal draws and solved for
$\beta_0$ by bisection. The intercepts were computed once, after
`set.seed(447)`, and saved, so every replicate uses the same truth
(@tbl-beta0).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-beta0
#| tbl-cap: "True intercepts used in the simulation. The slopes are the same in every column of a row."
b <- beta0
b$prev.lab <- pct(b$prev)
w <- reshape(b[, c("prev.lab", "sep.level", "beta0")], idvar = "sep.level",
             timevar = "prev.lab", direction = "wide")
names(w) <- sub("beta0.", "", names(w))
w$sep.level <- ifelse(w$sep.level == "low", "Low (s = 0.5)", "High (s = 1.5)")
names(w)[1] <- "Separation"
w[, -1] <- lapply(w[, -1], function(v) sprintf("%.2f", v))
kable(w, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr")
```

We varied three factors: prevalence $\pi$ (50%, 20%, 5% and 1%), training-set
size $n$ (1,000 and 20,000) and separation $s$ (0.5 and 1.5), which gives
$4 \times 2 \times 2 = 16$ settings. Each setting has $B = 100$ replicates,
so 1,600 training sets in all, enough for Monte Carlo errors small enough to
detect differences of 0.005. Each replicate also gets its own fresh test set
of 20,000 rows from the same model. The test set is used only to score the
final predictions, never for tuning.

The two sample sizes were chosen deliberately. At 1% prevalence,
$n = 1{,}000$ gives about 10 positives, few in *number*, while
$n = 20{,}000$ gives about 200: the same small *proportion*, but enough to
learn from. Comparing the two tells us whether a remedy is fixing a shortage
of positives or a lack of balance.

The seed is 447, set once in `R/00_setup.R`. Row $i$ of the design gets seed
$447 + i$, and method $j$ within that replicate gets seed $100(447 + i) + j$.
So all twelve methods (two classifiers, six approaches each) see exactly the
same training and test data in a given replicate, which lets us compare them
replicate by replicate. It also means the results do not depend on the order
in which the methods are run or on how many processor cores are used.

## A first look at the simulated data {#sec-simeda}

@fig-simdata plots simulated data from every setting. Because the slopes are
fixed, the positives always sit in the same direction, towards large values
of $x_1 - x_2$. Lowering the intercept does not move them; it just leaves
fewer of them. With low separation the two classes are mixed together even
when they are balanced.

![Simulated data in each setting, 3,000 points per panel. Positives (orange) always lie in the same direction; at lower prevalence there are simply fewer of them. Low separation (bottom row) mixes the classes more.](figures/fig1_simulated_imbalance.png){#fig-simdata width=88%}

@fig-simprob looks at the same data through the true probabilities, and it
shows why the 0.5 cutoff fails. At 50% prevalence about half of all cases
have a true probability above 0.5. At 1% prevalence and high separation only
0.14% of cases do, and even among the actual positives only about 10% have a
true probability above 0.5. With low separation the share is zero. In other
words, at low prevalence even a *perfect* model that knew the true
probabilities would almost never flag anything at a cutoff of 0.5. Low
sensitivity at that cutoff is a property of the cutoff, not a sign that the
model is broken, and that idea runs through the rest of the report.

![Distribution of the true probability $P(y = 1 \mid x)$ in 20,000 simulated cases per setting. The dashed line is the usual 0.5 cutoff. As positives become rarer, nearly every case falls below it.](figures/fig9_eda_simulated.png){#fig-simprob width=88%}

Before running the study we also checked that the generator produced what we
asked for (@tbl-sanity). In every setting the training prevalence, averaged
over replicates, is within 0.002 of the target. The smallest training set had
only 3 positives (1%, $n = 1{,}000$, low separation), which is exactly the
kind of situation in which people reach for a remedy. The table also gives the
Bayes benchmark, the ROC-AUC and PR-AUC of the true probabilities, which is
the best any method can do. ROC-AUC hardly changes with prevalence, but PR-AUC
drops sharply as positives become rare, which is why we report both measures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sanity
#| tbl-cap: "Generator check: observed training prevalence (mean over 100 replicates) and the Bayes benchmark (mean over both sample sizes)."
bay <- sim[sim$approach == "bayes", ]
bay$obs.prev <- bay$train.positives / bay$n
op <- aggregate(obs.prev ~ prev + sep.level + n, bay, mean)
op <- reshape(op, idvar = c("prev", "sep.level"), timevar = "n", direction = "wide")
fp <- aggregate(train.positives ~ prev + sep.level, bay[bay$n == 1000, ], min)
ba <- aggregate(cbind(roc.auc, pr.auc) ~ prev + sep.level, bay, mean)
s <- merge(merge(op, fp), ba)
s <- s[order(-s$prev, s$sep.level), ]
out <- data.frame(Target = pct(s$prev),
                  Separation = s$sep.level,
                  `Observed, n = 1,000` = sprintf("%.4f", s$obs.prev.1000),
                  `Observed, n = 20,000` = sprintf("%.4f", s$obs.prev.20000),
                  `Fewest positives (n = 1,000)` = s$train.positives,
                  `Bayes ROC-AUC` = f3(s$roc.auc),
                  `Bayes PR-AUC` = f3(s$pr.auc),
                  check.names = FALSE)
kable(out, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrrr")
```

## Real data: credit card fraud {#sec-realdata}

The real data are the Kaggle "Credit Card Fraud Detection" data, released by
the Machine Learning Group of the Université Libre de Bruxelles with
@dalpozzolo2015 and available at
<https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud>. They contain
284,807 card transactions made by European cardholders over two days in
September 2013; 492 of them (0.173%) are fraud. There are 30 predictors.
`V1` to `V28` are principal components that the data owners computed to
protect confidentiality, so they have no direct meaning. `Time` is the number
of seconds since the first transaction and `Amount` is the transaction
amount. There are no missing values. The file is about 150 MB, so it is not
stored on GitHub; the repository's README explains where to download it.

We made 10 random 70/30 train/test splits. Each split is stratified, meaning
frauds and normal transactions are sampled separately, so every training set
has 344 frauds and every test set has 148. `Time` and `Amount` are on much
larger scales than the principal components and would dominate the distances
that SMOTE uses, so we standardized them with the training-set mean and
standard deviation (applied to both halves). The principal components were
left as supplied. Split $k$ uses seed $447 + 10{,}000 + k$, and methods within
a split are seeded as in the simulation, so every method sees the same splits.

Two practical problems came up. First, `cv.glmnet()` did not converge at the
smallest values of its default $\lambda$ path, which runs down to $10^{-4}$
times the largest $\lambda$, where the fit is almost unpenalized. We used a
shorter, finer path of 200 values ending at $10^{-3}$ times the largest
$\lambda$. Second, a random forest with 200 trees on about 199,000 training
rows is slow, so each tree was grown on a sample of 20,000 rows instead of a
full bootstrap sample. This choice turns out to matter, and we come back to it
in @sec-reconcile.

## A first look at the credit card data {#sec-realeda}

Because the principal components cannot be interpreted, we explored the two
predictors that can, `Amount` and `Time` (@fig-ccdata). Panel A shows that
frauds are not simply large transactions. The median fraud is \$9.25 against
\$22.00 for a normal transaction, half of all frauds are under \$10, and 5.5%
of frauds are for \$0, compared with 0.6% of normal transactions. One
possible explanation is that a stolen card is first tried with a small
charge before it is used for larger ones. Frauds are also spread over the whole range of amounts, so
amount alone cannot separate the classes.

Panel B shows transactions per hour (grey bars) and the fraud rate in each
hour (orange). Activity follows a clear daily cycle, from about 1,100
transactions an hour at night to almost 10,000 during the day. The fraud
rate is highest at night, reaching 1.3% and 2.1% in two night-time hours,
compared with 0.17% overall, because fraud continues while normal spending
stops. So the level of imbalance is not even constant within the data: it
depends on when a transaction happens. Among the principal components, the
ones most correlated with fraud are `V17`, `V14`, `V12` and `V10` (correlations
between $-0.22$ and $-0.33$), so the information about fraud is spread across
several components rather than concentrated in one.

![Credit card data. A: distribution of transaction amount by class (log scale). B: number of transactions per hour (grey bars, right axis) and fraud rate per hour (orange, left axis) over the two days; the dashed line is the overall fraud rate of 0.17%.](figures/fig10_eda_creditcard.png){#fig-ccdata width=88%}
